title: Persistence: reading and writing files
summary: Save text to files and read it back safely, so data outlives the program.

sources.section: Reading Data From A Text File

license: Original work for Python Intelligence; license to be chosen by the owner
objective: Read and write text files safely with `with`, choosing the right mode for writing, appending and reading.
analogy: Opening a file is borrowing a library book: `with` makes sure it's handed back (closed) even if something goes wrong.

misconceptions.belief: Mode "w" adds to the end of a file.
misconceptions.correction: "w" empties the file first; use "a" to append.

misconceptions.belief: Lines read from a file have no newline.
misconceptions.correction: Reading keeps each line's "\n" where there is one (the last line may have none); strip it if you don't want it.

misconceptions.belief: Forgetting to close a file is harmless.
misconceptions.correction: Unclosed files may not be fully written; `with` closes them for you.

rubric.evidence: every file is opened in a with block
write replaces, append adds, read reads
newlines are written and stripped where the task asks, and a missing file is handled

review.recall: What is the difference between modes "w", "a" and "r"? Why use `with open(...)`?

steps.title: Data that outlives the program
steps.body:
Everything your programs have computed so far vanished when they finished. A to-do list, a game's high
score or a day's measurements are only useful if they are still there tomorrow. **Files** store text
on disk so another run, or another program, can read it back.

(Here, files live in your browser's memory, and every run starts in a fresh, empty folder, so each run
of your code begins with no files.)

steps.title: Open, work, close
steps.body:
Working with a file is like borrowing a notebook: you **open** it for reading or for writing, read or
write through a file object that keeps your place, and **close** it so the changes are saved and the
notebook goes back on the shelf.

Forgetting to close is easy, so Python offers `with`: the file is closed automatically when the
indented block ends, even if an error happens inside it.

questions: Why does it matter whether a file is closed, if the program is about to finish anyway?
What should happen to a file's old contents when you open it to write?

steps.title: Watch a file being written and read
steps.body: Two `with` blocks: one writes two lines, the other reads them back.

visual.code:
with open("todo.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("milk\n")
    f.write("eggs\n")

with open("todo.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip())

frames.note: Mode "w" creates the file (or empties an existing one) for writing.
`write` adds exactly the text given. The newline is part of the string.
The second line follows the first.
The first block ended, so the file was closed and saved. Now it is reopened for reading (the default mode).
Looping over a file gives one line at a time, newline included; `strip` removes it.
The second line. After the loop, `with` closes the file.

steps.title: The precise rules
steps.body:
`open(path, mode, encoding="utf-8")` returns a file object. Common modes: `"r"` read (the
default), `"w"` write (creates the file, or **erases** an existing one), `"a"` append to the end.

1. Pass `encoding="utf-8"` for text files: without it, the encoding depends on the platform.
2. `f.read()` returns the whole file as one string; `f.readline()` the next line; `for line in f:`
   visits each line in turn. Lines keep their trailing `\n`.
3. `f.write(text)` writes exactly `text` (no newline is added) and returns the number of characters.
4. `with open(...) as f:` closes the file when the block ends, even if an exception is raised.
5. Opening a missing file for reading raises `FileNotFoundError`. A relative path such as
   `"data.txt"` is looked up in the current working directory.

steps.title: Run it: a tiny score file
steps.body: Write, append, read back, and handle a missing file. Predict both lines first.
steps.code:
with open("scores.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("ana,7\nbo,9\n")
with open("scores.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("cy,4\n")

total = 0
with open("scores.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        name, score = line.strip().split(",")
        total = total + int(score)
print(total)

try:
    open("missing.txt", encoding="utf-8")
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("no such file")

steps.title: Your turn: count the non-blank lines
steps.body:
Complete `count_lines(path)` so it returns how many lines of the file contain something other than
spaces. Use `with` and `encoding="utf-8"`. A missing file should raise `FileNotFoundError` as usual.
hints: Open the file in a `with` block and loop over its lines.
Count a line when `line.strip()` is not empty.

tests.name: skips blank lines
tests.code:
with open('t1.txt', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as _f:
    _f.write('a

  
b
')
assert count_lines('t1.txt') == 2, f"got {count_lines('t1.txt')!r}"

tests.name: last line without newline
tests.code:
with open('t3.txt', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as _f:
    _f.write('x\ny')
assert count_lines('t3.txt') == 2, f"got {count_lines('t3.txt')!r}"

tests.name: missing file raises

steps.title: Challenge: a message log
steps.body:
Write two functions. `append_log(path, message)` adds `message` as a new line at the **end** of the file
(creating it if needed). `read_log(path)` returns the list of messages exactly as they were given (keep any spaces; drop only the
newline), or `[]` if
the file doesn't exist yet. The starter has two bugs; find them.
hints: Which mode adds to the end instead of erasing the file?
What happens when `read_log` is called before anything was logged? Catch that specific error.

tests.name: one line per message
tests.code:
append_log('log3.txt', 'x')
with open('log3.txt', encoding='utf-8') as _f:
    assert _f.read() == 'x\n', 'each message should end with exactly one newline'

tests.name: keeps spaces in messages
tests.code:
append_log('log4.txt', '  indented  ')
assert read_log('log4.txt') == ['  indented  '], f"got {read_log('log4.txt')!r}; remove only the newline, e.g. with rstrip('\\n')"

steps.title: Transfer: a notes file
steps.body:
Write `save_notes(path, notes)`, which writes each note on its own line, replacing anything in the file; `add_note(path,
note)`, which adds one note at the end without losing the others; and `read_notes(path)`, which returns the notes as a
list of strings without their newlines, or an empty list if the file doesn't exist yet.
hints: `with open(path, "w") as f:` then `f.write(note + "\n")` for each note; "a" instead of "w" to append.
Read with `[line.rstrip("\n") for line in f]`, inside `try`/`except FileNotFoundError: return []`.

tests.name: save then read
tests.code:
save_notes('n.txt', ['buy milk', 'call Sam'])
assert read_notes('n.txt') == ['buy milk', 'call Sam'], read_notes('n.txt')

tests.name: adding keeps the others
tests.code:
save_notes('n.txt', ['a'])
add_note('n.txt', 'b')
add_note('n.txt', 'c')
assert read_notes('n.txt') == ['a', 'b', 'c'], read_notes('n.txt')

tests.name: one note per line on disk
a missing file means no notes
notes come back exactly, spaces and empty notes included
tests.code:
notes = ['  indented', '', 'trailing space ']
save_notes('n.txt', notes)
assert read_notes('n.txt') == notes, read_notes('n.txt')
add_note('n.txt', ' spaced ')
add_note('n.txt', '')
assert read_notes('n.txt') == notes + [' spaced ', ''], read_notes('n.txt')

questions.prompt: You open an existing file with mode "w". What happens to its contents?
choices: They are kept; writes go at the end
questions.explanation: "w" truncates the file; use "a" to append.

questions.prompt: After `f.write("hi")` and closing, what does the file contain?
questions.explanation: `write` adds exactly the text you give it; newlines must be written explicitly.

questions.prompt: What is true right after a `with open(...) as f:` block ends?
questions.explanation: `with` closes the file at the end of the block (the name `f` still exists).

questions.prompt: What does each `line` contain in `for line in f:`?
choices: The text with its trailing newline (except possibly the last)
questions.explanation: Lines keep their `\n`; the last line may lack one if the file doesn't end with a newline.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.body:
- Open files with the right mode ("r", "w", "a") and `encoding="utf-8"`.
- Read a whole file, one line, or every line in a loop; write exactly the text you mean.
- Use `with` so files are always closed, and handle `FileNotFoundError` when a file may be missing.
